utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-04-75-T, The Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. It's Matthew Gillett, together with Senior Trial Attorney, Douglas Stringer, and legal intern Nika Jurkovic for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Strbac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still under oath. Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed. Sorry, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Strbac.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have the witness's statement, please, on the screen. It's 1D3652. And if there is a hard copy, that would be appreciated for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Strbac, in the very limited time remaining, I just want to ask you about two remaining issues, the first arising from paragraph 47 of your statement in which you describe the Croatian side arresting individuals in order to make up enough numbers to make a one-for-one exchange for the Croat prisoners held by the Serb side, and you describe here in paragraph 47 a particular way in which they were doing that; namely, arresting civilians on the Croatian side. Were there other ways that they increased the numbers of prisoners that they had to exchange?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mention in my statement, and I will repeat it now, that most often these civilians were said to be snipers, especially in 1993. There were many elderly people and even women about whom we asked when they were brought for exchange. They told us that they had been shooting from their apartments and houses, from windows, at soldiers and even civilians, men, women, and children. When they brought elderly people for exchange, I asked why, and they told me, They are snipers. So that was a bit ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. My question was whether there were other ways, aside from arresting elderly people who were civilians, were there other ways that they increased the numbers to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. They arrested, for instance, ex-officers, retirees. I remember there was some Pavle Osanica [phoen] in Zadar, born in Serbia but then moved to Croatia and stayed in Croatia because his wife was Croat and he had children there. Twice they brought him for exchange and twice he returned to Zadar. The third time they arrested him and we are still looking for him today. He didn't come to the Serbian side, but his family received information that he had been on his way to Zagreb when he reached Mount Velebit, and there he went missing without a trace. We are still looking for him. There were other arrests of shepherds, for instance. The Croatian army would raid these peripheral areas and they would arrest people who were tending to their sheep and cattle. We have such information. There are three ongoing tries. Croats are trying people who tortured people in jails. There were rapes. There were many arrests of civilians, shepherds, women, elderly men. I wrote a lot about that and published several books.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have 1D3786, please, which is Defence tab 75.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is a wire report apparently from Reuters, the 5th of November. At the top there's an indication it's 1993. It says: "United Nations and Serb officials have accused Croats of abducting rebel Serbs from Croatia's breakaway Krajina enclave. They say that those seized are used by the Croats to swell the numbers in prisoner exchanges. A UN official said abductions began at the end of last May. Abduction of Serb settlers by Croats in bordering villages in Sector South of the UN protected areas is becoming almost a regular practice, Heather Felsinger, a humanitarian officer with the UN Protection Force, told Reuters." And then you're quoted down at the bottom as saying: "We did not want to talk a lot about this problem as we didn't want to endanger the exchange of POWs." Now, can I just ask you this question, Mr. Strbac: How were these abductions possible given that they were in areas that were supposedly protected by the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, very simple. I explained yesterday that the UN was not deployed along borders. They only had a few check-points along borders. They were deployed in Krajina along the principle of ink spots -- inkblot pattern, so they were scattered all over. As for UNPROFOR, as far as UNPROFOR is concerned, the Croats could get in freely, the Croat army, police, et cetera. The Serbs were guarded by UN soldiers, which didn't offer much protection. I told you yesterday about Mirlovic Polje where seven elderly people were killed, including four women. This happened in the end of May, when in the village of Donji Baljci, Drnis municipality, they arrested seven shepherds, including two women, and I believe it was on 18 September that convictions were pronounced against some Croats, including one man called Jakovlovic, for torturing and raping the women. The verdict has not been written out yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were you aware and were other Serb officials aware that these abductions were occurring at the time?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware of them all. Sooner or later we'd find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If I can just go to my next question. Why didn't the Serb police or other forces stop them from occurring?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were not enough people. You must realise the length of the border between Republika Srpska Krajina and Croatia, I don't believe there is a longer border for such small countries, such small regions. We did not have enough personnel to protect, to defend, every metre of the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we do object on the basis of what this document goes to. Again, this goes to tu quoque evidence. It's about the purported abduction of Serbs. Now, the jurisprudence here at the Tribunal says that in general tu quoque evidence is not admissible, but there are exceptions where it has been shown there is a specific geographic and temporal link to crimes alleged in the indictment or the responsibility of the accused for those crimes. And I'm referring, for example, to a decision from the Prlic case of 17 August 2009, and can you see that on page 10, paragraph 23, of that decision. The Defence has not demonstrated how these purported border abductions have any impact on the crimes alleged against Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's step back and think about some of the evidence that was presented by the Prosecution in this case concerning the mission of the United Nations, whether and how they were able to defend certain areas, and the reasonableness and the explanation for the Serb side not disarming. There was a tremendous amount of evidence heard about that issue, and it is more than reasonable and perfectly relevant to present evidence suggesting that there was a real threat, firstly, that was not being responded to by the UN forces; that the RSK forces had good reason and the RSK government had good reason not to disarm in these areas. And, furthermore, in addition to this, the capacity of the Serb police and the Serb forces even to guard against infiltrations by Croat forces and to prevent crimes in the same areas where the Prosecution is arguing that those same forces could have prevented crimes against Croats and didn't do so for the deliberate purpose of encouraging their expulsion. Now, these matters are relevant, and I would suggest if this type of document, if this information is deemed irrelevant, as the Prosecution seems to wish, then Your Honours will be left with an extremely distorted, partial and incorrect view of the situation and the reasons for decisions by the RSK government.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And just one additional note. If the Defence is, indeed, conceding that there was a policy on the part of the RSK authorities not to disarm their forces, then we would withdraw the objection to the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection overruled. The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D3786 will be Exhibit D246.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have 1D2845, which is Defence tab 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, just to be clear from the outset, I don't intend to go into the substance of this document with you in any detail. I simply want to ask you this: Are you familiar with the contents of this report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I published it several times. I made it public.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When did you receive it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a few days after it was drafted, and if I remember well, it was written in October 1993. I received it directly from representatives of UNPROFOR. As I told you, I was part of the authorities. In addition to being secretary of the government, I was also chairman of that humanitarian commission of Krajina, or whatever you want to call it, commission for the exchange of prisoners, commission for the exchange of mortal remains, commission for humanitarian issues. In any case, I co-operated with representatives of international organisations and they insisted that after such a heinous crime such as the one in the Medak pocket, on at least making available to us the documentation they were able to collect if they were not able to protect us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And are the contents of this report generally accurate, based upon what you know about the events at Medak pocket?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that basically, yes. If we went into detail, I could tell you about certain things that were different, but basically 99 per cent is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: For the record, again, we'll put our objection about the tu quoque nature. And just do I understand correctly that the witness reads English as we've just seen an English version of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, is there a Serbian translation of this document?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The UNPROFOR made it and provided it. But I understand English enough to know that it concerns the Medak operation, and I know this document very well. I published it several times, both in English and in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, I tender this document. I will undertake to attempt to obtain the B/C/S version as well so that can be uploaded, for what it's worth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 1D2845 will be Exhibit D247.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That concludes my direct examination, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Strbac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If I could just take a minute to rearrange my affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Take your time. Let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Strbac. As you're probably aware, my name is Matthew Gillett. I'm representing the Prosecution. I'm going to ask you some questions. If any of them are unclear, please ask me to clarify, and I'll endeavour to do so. Now, firstly, yesterday you spoke about the powers of the RSK president under the constitution, and at transcript page 12460, you said that: "In times of the state of war or imminent threat of war, he assumed the powers of the parliament and transferred them to the government." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's roughly it, essentially. Maybe there are some nuances, but basically that's it. Perhaps I could tell you in which way he transferred those powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We will get to the nuances. My question was whether you recall saying that, that portion that I quoted from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, yes, roughly, that's it. Basically that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get L3, page 23 in the English, on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And so this is the RSK constitution which you were shown yesterday. Now, Hadzic, he assumed the powers of the assembly in accordance with Article 78, paragraph 7, of the constitution, as I understand, and I'll read this paragraph. It says: "Under his initiative or under the government's proposal, during a state of war or immediate threat of war, adopts acts about issues from the assembly's jurisdiction and is required to submit them before the assembly as soon as the assembly is able to meet. Acts adopted during the state of war may limit certain human and civil rights and liberties and change the organisation structure and authority of the government and its ministries, courts and public prosecutor's offices." That is the provision under which he assumed the powers of the assembly in a state of war or imminent threat of war; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And the government acted pursuant to the authority that Hadzic delegated to it. For example, as you said in a decision in September 1993 concerning the appointment of judges in the RSK, that was based on his presidential decree from January; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And the presidential decree you were referring to was the one of 22 January 1993 proclaiming a state of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: For the record, that's P2742.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recall that after the Miljevac Plateau incident in June 1992, the RSK declared an imminent state of war?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I didn't see that document during proofing. I allow the possibility that it is so, but I can't be positive. If you have the document, please show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Is it fair to say your recollection of events in June 1992 is somewhat faded?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, concerning that document that you're asking me about, I really can't remember. It faded in my memory. But as for the other question, every year my organisation and I organise memorial services for all these events, including the Medak pocket. And we have published a lot of documents, although I can't remember this particular one. I'm inclined to think that it was not published because we have a decree from January 1993, and it would have been logical - although I can't remember precisely - that the imminent threat of war had not been proclaimed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could get P2742, and this is the presidential decree of 22 January 1993, on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And, sir, if we look at point 1, we see that he says: "I declare a state of war throughout the state territory of the RSK." And then at point 2, he says: "I order a general mobilisation according to the Defence plan." And do you see his signature there on the document?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And this was sent out to the Main Staff of the Army of the RSK, the prime minister of the RSK, and the minister of interior; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, while Hadzic delegated some of the assembly powers to the government under his war powers, he still issued decrees himself; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. That assumes facts not in evidence. The characterisation has been made about -- well, I'll withdraw that objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, could you answer my question.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was adopted on the 22nd of January. I believe it's the same date as the decree we just discussed. So it was the same day that both documents were passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry to cut you off, and there was an exchange back and forwards so I'll repeat my question, which is: While Hadzic, as president, delegated some of the assembly powers to the government pursuant to his war powers, he still issued decrees himself after and on 22 January 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I do object to that one, Mr. President. That does assume a fact that is not in evidence because the proposition embedded in the question is that some powers of the assembly are being exercised by the president and that he is issuing decrees in those areas, and that's not been put to the witness. That particular aspect has not been put to the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, given that the witness is a lawyer and former judge, if we're going to discuss this in further detail, and given that it appears that he does understand some English, I would have to ask him to leave the courtroom. But to put my answer succinctly, I would say that the preceding questions did, indeed, establish the basis for this question, and beyond that, this is cross-examination. So I'm entitled to put whichever proposition is based on the provisions that we're seeing in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is -- sorry, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I just wanted to say, Mr. President, that even though it's cross-examination, there still is a need to establish the predicates to questions. That's still a requirement and that's the basis of the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So I'll repeat my question again. While Hadzic, as president, had delegated some of the assembly powers to the government, he still issued decrees pursuant to his war-time power; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I saw some documents. I cannot remember right now. I've already told you that this document bears the same date as that decree transferring powers. Of course, the president could, formally speaking, always take back the powers that he transferred to someone else. I don't remember that, though. If you have a document to that effect, I can tell you, as a lawyer. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay. Could we get P998. And this is tab 25, page 62, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And, sir, while this is coming up, I note that you referred to the removal of the RSK prime minister, Zdravko Zecevic, and his replacement by Bjegovic in your statement. And this occurred at the same time that you became secretary of the government; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, what we have coming up on the screen are the minutes from the extraordinary session of the RSK Assembly of 17 -- 27 March 1993. And on this page, we see Hadzic's decision as president of 17 March 1993 which is read out. This has been read out by chairman Mile Paspalj and the decision says: "The current prime minister of RSK, Zdravko Zecevic, MA, is hereby removed from office, effective 17 March 1993." That's correct, that Hadzic removed Zecevic on 17 March 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this document, that seems to be it. A month later, I became the secretary of the government. The government itself appoints the secretary. So once the government was formed, they appointed me secretary. That was a month after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered the question. Hadzic's decision that we see of 17 March 1993 was a war-time decree; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to be that way because a state of war was declared in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, if we could move to page 59 of the English in this, and this is page 49 of the B/C/S on the right-hand side, we see the debates concerning Hadzic's decision to remove Zecevic and we see that one of the assembly members said the following: "Zecevic perhaps wanted to introduce order. I may not even agree with the president of the republic, but inside this assembly, I have to, because ultimately Mr. Hadzic is president of the republic." This member stated that he was compelled to accept the decision of Mr. Hadzic because of his office of president; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to find it. Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: In the English, it is the second-to-bottom paragraph. In the B/C/S -- do you see it now?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is it, so Zecevic is not the one who was supposed to resolve everything and within that context even the president of the republic and the president of the assembly are guilty --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. It's the --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, is it this? "Perhaps Zecevic is the least guilty of all. Only time will tell. Zecevic perhaps wanted to introduce order. I may not even agree with the president of the republic, but inside this assembly, I have to, because after all Mr. Hadzic is the president of the republic." Well, in Serbian, this doesn't sound as if he has to vote for Hadzic's proposal. In Serbian, it doesn't sound that way. He says: "I may disagree with the president of the republic, but I have to agree in this assembly because, after all, Mr. Hadzic is the president of the republic." From this, we only see that he respects that high office and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, you never met Hadzic, as far as you recall, correct, face to face?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, during the war, certainly not. After the war, we went our separate ways as refugees. Of course, I'd recognise him anywhere in the world because I saw him in the media a lot, and he probably saw me quite a bit, too. I do not remember meeting him, encountering him, exchanging greetings, saying hello, hello. I don't even remember speaking to him on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And you do not know what interactions he was having with other members of the RSK government, do you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. What did not go through me as secretary of the government or through Savo Strbac as a personality, I really don't know. How could I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So you don't know what influence Hadzic was having on government decisions, do you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That would not be right. I was secretary of the government, and if something would arrive through official channels, then I'd have to know about that. If you are now trying to ask me whether indirectly he called one of the ministers and influenced him in order to have this or that decision reached, I don't know. I really do not know, and I cannot answer that kind of question because, after all, that's a hypothetical question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now get P999 on the monitor, please. And this is tab 33. If we could get page 26 of the English, and this is B/C/S pages 56 to 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement and in your evidence, you've described some problems that the RSK government had and you mention this in multiple places. The document that's coming up in front of us is the record of the 1st Session of a Conference of the Assembly of the RSK on 9 October 1993, and I'm interested in a portion where Milan Martic describes some of the problems in the RSK. His speech starts at page 21, but looking at page 26, we see, and I quote, starting from, "On the whole," which is in the middle of the page: "On the whole, the Serb Krajina republic's president, Goran Hadzic, stayed in Krajina for one hour every two months, and he could hardly bear even that one hour so had to run back saying that he did not have a place to stay there. I told him that we had rented a house for him. We were a paying the rent for six or seven months for nothing. The government paid simply because he could not be in Knin." And then if I skip further: "The reason that the government has not been competent is that it was being obstructed by President Hadzic and the group around him. It was not the government that has had the Serb Krajina republic's financial resources at its disposal but the group around President Hadzic." That is one of the reasons for the RSK government's problems, to the extent there were problems, correct, the behaviour of Hadzic and his associates?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the opinion of Mr. Martic who, at the time, was minister of the interior, as far as I can remember, in Bjegovic's government. So, as for his opinion, I really have no comment on that, except that's the opinion of a minister. And Hadzic rarely went to Knin; there's no denying that. Everybody knows that. I spoke about that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm interested in your opinion. Is it true that the misbehaviour of Hadzic and his associates was a cause of the problems of the RSK government?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bjegovic government, no. As far as I can remember, it was an excellent team, if I may say so. In, say, 90 per cent of all cases, decisions were made unanimously. However, Hadzic was president before that as well during the Zecevic government, so -- well, Martic was in the Zecevic government, too, so perhaps something from that period. I mean, he could have presented his views. As far as I can remember, there were ministers from the eastern part, from Eastern Slavonia, where Hadzic lived and worked, but these ministers were very devoted to Prime Minister Bjegovic. I knew them personally. They were a very good team and they became even closer because of war and all the trouble that followed. So in my opinion, there was nothing that would indicate that Hadzic was exerting any kind of pressure on any minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, that's not the question that I asked. You've referred to the prior period during the Zecevic government, but this statement comes from the period during the Bjegovic government. Are you saying that it is not true that Hadzic's and his associates' behaviour had a negative impact on the functioning of the RSK government during that period?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection; vague. But now not only is it all behaviour being referred to but also all associates, and that's a very wide range, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you rephrase, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, are you saying that Martic's claims here at the assembly in October 1993 that the conduct of Hadzic and the group around him was having a negative impact on the functioning of the RSK government is not true?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just saying that I did not notice any influence over the members of the government while I was there, that is to say, from April, I mean when this session was held. Now, whether Hadzic influenced some other structures of authority -- there's the army, there's the police, like in any other country. It's not only the government. They're not only ministers who are members of the government. There are other structures as well. Whether objectively he could have exercised any influence, in all sincerity, I don't think so. I don't think that Karadzic could have influenced anybody or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You said Karadzic. I believe you mean Hadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hadzic, Hadzic, Hadzic. I'm sorry, it was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, prior to this quote I've just read from minister of the interior Milan Martic, Martic said about Hadzic: "He is surrounded by a group so deep into crime that he could absolutely never get away from it." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. Objection, Mr. President. It's vague as to whether what's being asked is that that's what said or is that the way it was. That needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm asking him whether that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Martic said that, if that is what is written here, then that was it. I did not attend this session, this assembly, I think. I don't know whether Martic said it, but you and I and anybody else can read this. If it's written in the record, then it's written in the record. But it's a different matter whether that is what actually happened in real life, in reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: That isn't my question. Is that true, in reality, or is it not, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that nobody brought criminal charges against him during the war, and I know that he was not relieved of the duties of president because of some crimes. I know that where he was a candidate when he ran for the Presidency, he lost, but nobody prosecuted him for crimes. Both he and I lived in Serbia. I would have known had criminal charges been brought against him. As for rumours, I've already said that. After the war I heard these stories that Hadzic was linked to some kind of trade oak wood, whatever, in Slavonia. This is really just rumours. You said a moment ago that I'm a lawyer, that I was a judge for many years, and I cannot rely on rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, as secretary of government, your purview did not specifically relate to military affairs; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was an administrative person in the government. I did not have any ministry of my own. I was supposed to prepare sessions of the government, and then when a decision was made by the government, we should prepare everything to have such a decision published. And before that, I headed the government commission for humanitarian affairs, and that included the exchange of prisoners, the exchange of mortal remains, and exchanges of civilians, too, and also talking to all international organisations and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Thank you, sir. You don't know whether Hadzic issued military orders to the RSK forces, do you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know. I did not hear of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And at government sessions, that was never brought up, that he had issued any orders like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get P182. This is tab 15, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, this is an order by Hadzic dated 20 May 1993, so that's while you were the secretary of the government, and it's an order to expand the authority of supervising officers at the level of brigade and higher. Do you see the order on the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: This is an exercise of Hadzic's war-time powers; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this, that would seem be to the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, turning to a new topic, you've mentioned your work as a lawyer. And you were working as a lawyer in 1991 and 1992 and thereafter in the RSK; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: One of your previous clients was a Nikola Gagic; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And he was convicted of murdering two Croats in Prizren, near Benkovac, in November 1991 at first instance; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wife was a Serb and the husband was a Croat. My friends. I knew them personally. While I was a judge at the municipal court in Benkovac, that man was a lay judge, and while I worked in a company, the son of the woman was the director of that company. It was a second marriage for both of them. I'm speaking about the victims, of course. I knew them very well. And, yes, I defended Gagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, a correction for the record. The last document is not from 1993 but from 1992, and it was represented to the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, yes, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- represented to the witness ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett, does that change anything to your assertion that this document was from the time Mr. Strbac was secretary of the government?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. It does affect the fact that he was secretary of the government. If we could get the document again back on the monitor, and indeed this is from 1992. This is P182, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, would you agree nonetheless that that this was an exercise of Hadzic's war-time powers?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But at that time a state of imminent threat of war or a state of war had not been declared. That happened only later in January 1993 when he transferred his powers to the government. So that is a significant difference in respect of what you tried to make me say, that it was 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are you saying that Hadzic could exercise his war-time powers in May 1992 even before the declaration of a state of war?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems to be that way. Well, now, we'd have to take a look at this together, what Article 78 says, whether it pertains to a state of war only or is it part of his regular powers, because the powers of the president of the state are defined in Article 78. We can go back to paragraph 12 and then we can take a look at this together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And you'll agree with me that this order says: "In order to eliminate the threat for the vital interests of the Republika Srpska Krajina and the interests of the Serb people on the whole by the fact of the state of war present in Republika Srpska Krajina, I issue the following ... order." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that the vital interests of the RSK would not be jeopardized. This can be interpreted in legal terms, that there was a war going on, but that does not mean that necessarily there had been a state of war declared. It is a fact that there was a war, that war was being waged, starting in 1991, but that does not mean that a state of war had been declared. Why would then somebody declare a state of war in January 1993 if it had been declared before that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And as you mentioned, the order refers to Article 78(12), clause 12, Hadzic could exercise this power even in the absence of a formal declaration of a state of war or an imminent state of war; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We'll agree on that, yes. But that's a completely different thing compared to what you asked me before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. If we could go back to the Gagic case, you were brought in as the defence counsel on the appeal; correct? Together with a Goran Majstorovic.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And the first-instance conviction of Gagic was overturned and sent back to be re-decided, and then the case was transferred back to the public prosecutor in Knin in July 1993. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knin? I'm not sure. But the appeal was successful and a retrial was granted, but I'm not sure whether it was in Knin or Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So you don't know whether the case was transferred back to the RSK courts.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly wasn't transferred back to the RSK. Those were military courts, both the lower and the higher. Up to May 1992, military courts held trials for crimes committed by soldiers, both in Serbia, in BH, and in RSK, and the military courts deferred cases to civilian courts after the army withdrew. I know that case very well, and the Croats cited it a million times. And I know what you're going to ask, so please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Well, first, could we get P3024 - and this is tab 93, page 6 - on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And, sir, this is a letter from the military court in Belgrade explaining the cessation of the military courts in Zagreb, Split and Sarajevo. On page 6, at point number 5, we see a reference to the Gagic case. Firstly, do you see that it says, in relation to the victims, "Miletic Kuzman and his wife Djuka, that they were civilians of Croat ethnicity ..." It's what it says there; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I told you they were my friends. She was a Serb. I know her entire family. This was their second marriage. They had no children in common.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can say whatever it wants. I know what I know. Djuka is a typically Serbian name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If I may then ask you, it says that the case was forwarded to the RSK public prosecutor in Knin after the military court in Belgrade was proclaimed incompetent. So you were not aware of that, were you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know on what grounds. You told me a moment ago that the conviction was repealed and the case was sent back for re-trial. It doesn't say that here. It says the case was forwarded to the public prosecutor in Knin after the court, the military court, pronounced itself incompetent. Why? I don't know. All I know is that the judgement was repealed and that at the re-trial I did not represent the Gagics.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, it's correct that the first-instance judgement was overturned and subsequently there was no re-trial because it was referred back to the public prosecutor in Knin. If we look now to the decision that you've mentioned by the Belgrade Supreme Court - this is 1D2523, which is tab 87 - and this is the decision of 7 May 1992. While this is coming up, does that date sound correct for the appeal decision that you were the defence counsel on?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. 19 May 1992 is the day when military courts lost jurisdiction in the RSK. It fits in, as far as dates are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 of the English, in the middle of the first paragraph on page 2, it's listing the arguments of the defence in this case. If we could go to page 2 of the English. Sorry, this is page 3 of the English, and the first -- middle of the first paragraph, and this is page 3, third paragraph, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And as this comes up, it says: "Defence counsel considers that the conduct" -- this is about halfway down the first paragraph: "Defence counsel considers that the conduct of the accused was not unlawful because he committed the crime against persons whom he rightfully considered to be members of the other party to the conflict and a soldier is never held responsibile for killing an opponent. It is inconsequential that the injured parties had the status of civilians because we are talking about a civil war and enemy territory." Do you stand by that argument, that it's permissible to kill civilians in enemy territory during a time of war?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this is just as -- the supreme military court took something out of context from my appeal, which was several hundred pages long. But this was a statement wherein I, as a lawyer, as a human being, condemned during the war the makers of that war. I condemned in my appeal those who brought that young man, Gagic, who was just doing his military service, who brought him to the front line and told him, All of what you see in front of you are enemies. This young man was painted in camouflage, went to the other side, killed people, playing some Indian dance, shouting yoo hoo hoo, and then he was locked up by the Ustashas. I condemned those who brought that young man to the front line and told him, All you see facing you from the other side are enemies.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the interpreters ask you, once again, to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, my question was: Do you stand by the proposition that it's permissible to kill civilians during a time of war. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's one thing when you are in the role of defence counsel and another thing if you are a human being. My view is that it's not acceptable to kill anyone, let alone civilians. I dealt with humanitarian work but I was also a defence counsel. I defended people the best I could. Ultimately, you can see that the Supreme Court - and the Supreme Court is not just anyone - accepted my arguments and returned the case for re-trial. This is taken out of a broader context. I repeat: I'm against wars, against the killing of both soldiers and civilians. If I had any decision-making power, I would never send anyone to war. I lost a 10-and-a-half-year-old son during the war. I know what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You don't mention the Gagic case anywhere in your evidence or your statement, do you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I mention him? I defended him. At one point, as a lawyer, I had 35 clients in Krajina who were murderers. They were all ongoing cases. I didn't mention any case in which I acted as defence counsel. There was never any mention of it. I wasn't holding anything back. I wasn't concealing that I worked as a defence lawyer throughout the war, and I can even tell you that I had the honour of being a member of the bar association of Croatia and then the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and later of Serbia, and then the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So, yes, I worked as a lawyer in many states.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'd tender this judgement, 1D2523.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: To what end, Mr. Gillett?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We will not admit the document, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that this topic came up in the International Court of Justice proceedings. Serbia was so concerned about your reliability in these proceedings that it disavowed you as a witness; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who disavowed me?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are misinformed. It is the Croats who didn't want to hear any witnesses from the Serbian side. The Serbs put me forward and insisted. It was at the proposal of the Serbian side that eight witnesses were supposed to be heard. The Croats didn't want to hear any of them, and we still don't understand why the Croats didn't want to hear them. And they had special objections to my appearing as a witness because I was supposed to be an expert witness who collected documents and made a statement. My whole statement was admitted. I testified because my statement was relayed by a lawyer from the Serbian side. The Croats could have cross-examined me but they did not wish to for reasons only they know. It's not the Serbs who gave up on me. The Serbs built their cases primarily on the information that I provided, and it was included in the closing arguments and it was referred to throughout the trial. So you are misinformed, seriously misinformed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could I get 65 ter 6712, and this is tab 64, page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is available on the ICJ website. It is the rejoinder memorial of the Republic of Serbia, dated 1 November 2011, volume 1. If we go to page 3, we have the excerpt, and this is paragraph 592. And here's what Serbia said after discussing the Gagic judgement that we've just discussed: "Even if the military court interpreted the defence submission precisely, it should be noted that Mr. Strbac is not a witness, nor an expert witness, nor defence counsel in this case. He is merely the head of an NGO. It is the organisation and not Mr. Strbac personally that has collected evidence of the Serb victims in Croatia." So it's correct that Serbia disavowed your evidence and effectively dropped you as a witness, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you talking about, man? That's not the way it was. They can write anything. When this was written -- I don't know if you saw the rest of the material. The Croats appealed, we counterappealed, and then the Croats responded with the same arguments as you read out in the Gagic case and they wrote -- I mean, the Serbs then wrote what they wrote. After that, witnesses were proposed. So the Serbs are responding to Croat objections, Croat arguments. I don't see where you draw the conclusion from that they disavowed me. I think it was on 13 or 14 March - you can open the records of the International Court of Justice - where my statement was presented before the court by Counsel Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, if I could --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can look at that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: -- just cut in here. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so we don't waste any more time on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We would tender this as it goes directly to the witness's credibility, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Apologies, I see that we're not ready for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. I think that this passage has been mischaracterised by the Prosecution. There isn't sufficient context to understand precisely what's being said here, absolutely no indication that the witness was being effectively dropped, so this has no impeachment value.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we included the context, Serbia's argument concerning the Gagic issue, and where my learned friend says there is no indication he has been dropped, we would say that's contradicted by the express terms "Mr. Strbac is not a witness, nor an expert witness, nor defence counsel in this case," which are abundantly clear on their face as to what Serbia is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's quite different from saying that someone has been dropped as a witness. It's a factual statement about the status of a person who, for example, could be submitting an amicus brief, a report, something akin to a Brandeis brief. And the reason for his status at that stage could have been decided for reasons that have nothing whatsoever to do with his credibility, such as - and this is what the witness has said - that there was no objection apparently to tendering of his report, or there was no need for cross-examination. So there's not a sufficient basis for this to have any impeachment value.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Just as a note, Your Honours, this is why I said "effectively dropped," and the context in these surrounding pages makes it abundantly clear what Serbia is doing and the reasons for which it is doing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, you were a member of the Benkovac TO Staff in late 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1977, I was a member of the Benkovac TO Staff. 1977.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And you were still a member in late 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And you were an intelligence officer in the Benkovac TO Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Zoran Lekic was the commander of the Benkovac TO Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lakic. Zoran Lakic. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And the volunteers in the Benkovac TO Staff were headed by Zoran Tadic; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. Possibly. It must have been a short period of time. There was somebody called Zoran Tadic. We have a lot of Tadics in villages around Benkovac. I don't know if he was a volunteer or a local. But during those days of war, there was some Zoran Lakic who appeared at the staff or was attached to the staff. I don't know if he received any assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get 65 ter document 6720. This is tab 72. And could we get page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, if we look at number 26, that's you; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And then if we look number 28, that's Zoran Tadic; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says here that he was a commander. I told you, there was one Zoran Tadic. Whether a local or an outsider, I don't know. There are many people called Tadic in my village as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We would seek to admit this document 6720, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 6720 will be Exhibit P3317.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The chief of the public security branch in Benkovac was Bosko Drazic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And in November 1991, the 180th Motorised Brigade of the JNA was operating in the area of Benkovac; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I think that's what it's called. Traditionally there was a large military presence there from pre-war times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Benkovac is close to the village or town of Skabrnja; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Relatively. About 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And Skabrnja is close -- 3 or 4 kilometres from your home town where you were born of Rastevic; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rastevic. About 10 kilometres. If there's 10 kilometres from Benkovac and 6 from my village, then it must be between 10 and 15. But there are two villages in between, Zagradina and then Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And Nadin is also close to Benkovac; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all relative, yes. And it belonged to Benkovac municipality, Nadin did. And Skabrnja belonged to Zadar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, pre-war Skabrnja had about 2.000 inhabitants and was large majority Croat ethnicity; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Croats but I don't know how many. Since I didn't belong to Benkovac municipality, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you dispute that Skabrnja was an overwhelming majority Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, they were 99 per cent Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Serb forces attacked Skabrnja and Nadin on 18 October 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The JNA led the operation, as far as I heard. I wasn't a participant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The Benkovac TO was involved in the operation as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some parts. It's a very broad concept. Do you mean that these members of the staff participated? Maybe some of them did, but the majority didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The Serb forces killed several Croat civilians during the attack on Skabrnja and Nadin on 18 October 1991 and thereafter; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I turned over the mortal remains to the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could get P2647 - this is tab 12 - on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And this is a report from Lieutenant-Colonel Simo Rosic of the 180 Motorised Brigade concerning the killings of civilians in Skabrnja and Nadin. Now, if we look at page 1, second paragraph, he says that: "All the collected data shows that the killings were committed by members of the Benkovac TO Staff special units, or units that fought under their command. These were volunteers from Serbia and Opacic's group composed of combatants from the area." Who is the Opacic that he is referring to?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were several Opacics but you probably mean Goran Opacic. He was a policeman before the war - I don't know in which place - and he came to Benkovac, as many others who had been expelled from Croatia did. And allegedly a group of people gathered around him, tough guys mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: At page 2 of this report --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you straight away. I thought you were going to ask me something else. In relation to Skabrnja, there were many, many trials, and it was established that Opacic and his group did not take part in that action. So much for the authenticity of this document. I'm talking about verdicts by Croat courts, Croatian courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So are you sure that this is Goran Opacic that is being referred to? Are you now sure of that when you're referring to this document?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no other Opacic group, apart from the Goran Opacic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, at page 2 of the report, it notes that a Gjindic mutilated the body of one of the Croat victims by cutting off the ear and was showing this in cafes in Benkovac. You're aware of that, right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I don't rule out the possibility because there were lunatics on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, you don't mention anywhere in your statement or evidence the killing of Croat civilians by the Serb forces in Skabrnja and Nadin, do you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I mention it? I didn't take part in that operation. I turned over the mortal remains. I was already involved in exchanges by that time. I believe there were 48 sets of mortal remains to the Croats, and the Territorial Defence members pulled out villagers out of that village because the fighting was fierce. Over 100 women and children were brought to Benkovac in two buses, and the next day I turned them over to Croats --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- after we had arranged that exchange by telephone. And I don't see why I would tell what happened in Skabrnja in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, I see the time. As a final question, you weren't involved in the Medak pocket operation or the Miljevac operation either, but you choose to mention them in your evidence. And I put it to you that you don't mention the killing and mistreatment of Croat civilians because you're attempting to minimise the suffering of Croats and exaggerate the suffering of Serbs. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely wrong. In many other places, I spoke about that publicly, and I wrote about victims on the Croat side. I never said before but I'm telling you now that I turned over at least 48 victims to the Croats. So the Croats knew about all this. I arranged the hand-over with them. That is very well known. And all these civilians, women and children, I also turned them over one or two days after the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, we'll take the first break, 30 minutes, and we will come back at 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, we hear that you have a preliminary matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you and Your Honours. Just a housekeeping matter related to the previous witness. We've been informed by e-mail this morning that the Defence agrees that we can replace Exhibit P03081 with 65 ter 1597.2, and so we're requesting that now P3081 be replaced by 65 ter 1597.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that the amalgamated document we were talking about yesterday with Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. That can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, you were still a member of the Benkovac TO in March 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are you aware of a visit to this area by Goran Hadzic, Zdravko Zecevic, Milan Martic, and Arkan Raznjatovic around 13 March 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I cannot remember, especially not that they came that way together. No, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'll now turn to a new topic which is events in Ovcara in 1991, November. Now, sir, you're aware that the Serb forces killed over 200 Croat victims on 20 November 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Which part of that is not correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that I knew that they were killed then, in 1991, 1992. It's not correct that I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, but we'll move on. Sir, the Republika Srpska Krajina had a policy of not recognising responsibility for events occurring prior to the formation of the RSK; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. Quite frankly, I don't understand that question of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get 65 ter 6684, and I note that this is an article that is also contained in Defence document 1D2697. It's tab 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And, sir, this is an article from November 1993 in Vecernje Novosti. And at page 2 in the second-last paragraph, near the bottom - this is the middle column in B/C/S - there's a quote from yourself and it's concerning the events in Ovcara. Among other reasons, you say, "Our young state cannot be held responsible because it was still not formed at that time." You are referring to Republika Srpska Krajina here; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is that? I cannot see that actual quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: It should be the middle column in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I request that the column be expanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under my photograph, I don't know whether this has been translated. Do you see what I'm saying? It says "Our interlocutor claims that --" well, I don't know. You're trying to get me so say something about something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, it's the column which is now to the left in bold --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: -- and starting: "'Until 3 January 1992,'" it says, "'at the time that the Sarajevo agreement was signed and the decision adopted for the arrival of the Blue Helmets to the former Yugoslavia, the fighting was going on between the JNA and the Croatian army. For anything happening at that time, our young state cannot be held responsible because it was still not formed at that time, nor did it have its own army,' added Strbac." Did you state this?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And read out the next sentence in bold as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, you've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could now get -- and I will come back to this article. But, first, could we get P2249.2168.1, and this is tab 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: While this is coming up, this is a report from UN CIVPOL from November 1992, and at this time the Ovcara grave had been located and the internationals were attempting to get approval from the RSK authorities to carry out the exhumation. If we turn to page 2, and this is page 1 in B/C/S. On page 2 of the English, we see that it says, the sentence starting: "On the 28th October 1992, the local police told CIVPOL they were instructed not to investigate any matters which occurred prior to the establishment of the Serbian Republic of Krajina." That's in line with your comments in the previous article that we just saw; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot see it on this page of mine, so have them place the second page there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: This is at the bottom of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, but then it continues on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So this statement that the local police were instructed not to investigate anything which occurred prior to the formation of RSK, that's consistent with what you said publicly, that the RSK could not be responsible for events prior to its formation; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what was I then in 1992? If you think that somebody drew such conclusions on the basis of a public statement of mine, I mean, I really see no connection between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now get P3065. This is tab 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, this is a letter from Milan Ilic who was the president of the SBWS regional council of RSK, and it's a letter of 28 October 1992 responding to the internationals' requests to exhume Ovcara. Now, if we look at page 1, the second paragraph of this letter, he says that the attempts to investigate, and I'm paraphrasing, Ovcara were an attempt to "Satanise the Serbs." Then at point 2, if we jump down to point 2, he says: "The information is from part of the Croatian armed forces Ustasha who committed murder" --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No translation. No translation. Now it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Let me repeat that quote. He says: "The information is from part of the Croatian armed forces Ustasha who committed murder against civil inhabitants who have not been suitable for them till 17 October 1991 (till the fall of Vukovar), and buried them at this location willing now to push under our side better say the Serbs, their monstrous crime." He is suggesting that the crimes, the victims at Ovcara were victims of the Croatian side, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. Believe me, I have no idea what he is suggesting here. What does this have to do with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, this letter concerns the attempts to exhume Ovcara. Are you disagreeing that Ilic's words here suggest that it was the Croats who were responsible for this? Do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many people lost their lives on both sides in Vukovar. What he meant is something that he should be asked or whoever it was that drafted this. Many Serbs and Croats lost their lives in Vukovar. In 1991, the bloodiest war was waged precisely in the Vukovar area. There are many missing persons to this day. There were many killings that were committed, Ovcara and other ones. I didn't know about Ovcara people. We're referring to some kind of Ovcara but nobody knew whether it really existed and what it was all about. In 1997, a Serb was convicted for a killing and Ovcara was marked in a completely different place --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in a different place and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: -- we've gone somewhat off track, so we've gone somewhat off track here. You also said that the Croatian requests and the international attempts to exhume Ovcara were an effort to Satanise the Serb side, and you suggested that this was actually a Croatian conspiracy, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this is a quotation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If this is a quotation from the newspaper article in which the witness is quoted, I would say that that should be put on the screen for him to review, to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was first giving the witness a chance to see if he was willing to recall it off his own memory and then was going go to the specific quote and read out the quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So first I'd like to ask the witness whether he agrees that he also alleged the attempts to exhume Ovcara were an effort to Satanise the Serbs and were part of a Croatian conspiracy. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just said that I don't know about Ovcara. People were talking about some Ovcara. When I say that I didn't know about Ovcara, I didn't know what it contained - Serbs, Croats. People talked and then Ovcara means that there are some sheep there, and then people were saying that there were some dead sheep there. I mean, I didn't know what this was all about at this Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, if I may interrupt. If I may interrupt, you're not answering my question. My question is whether you recall making public statements that the efforts to exhume Ovcara were an attempt to Satanise the Serbs and part of a Croatian conspiracy. Do you recall that or do you not recall that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that. I do not recall that, really, that anything was said in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could go back to 6684, and again this is 1D2697 but 6684 is the shorter version. Page 2, right at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: In the preceding paragraph, it identifies yourself. It says: "Our interlocutor claims that the government committee was not aware whether the Ovcara grave contains what the Croatian propaganda is claiming. If there are bodies in it, they could also be bodies of Serbs because at least 97 Serbs are still missing from those territories. Speaking about the Vukovar tragedy, he said that the people in Krajina are convinced that this was a great trick against the Serb nation that had been directed by the military and state leadership of that time in order to Satanise the Serb nation in the eyes of the outside world." So you did state that Ovcara was an effort to Satanise the Serbs, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. Objection, Mr. President. You'll notice that the formulation of the -- by the witness has now been changed and subsumed under the word "Ovcara" by the Prosecutor's question. And there are many facets of that and so therefore that's not been put precisely to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we have the next page in English on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, if we look to the final paragraph, it says: "Leaving the possibility open that Ovcara might contain bodies, Strbac pointed out that the Serb side will still have a lot to offer to the international committee and that International Justice Tribunal because the Croatian side had shown the face of genocide in this war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The column really should be expanded so the witness can be reading along.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, I'll put it to you again, sir, that you did state that the efforts to exhume and to investigate the crimes at Ovcara were an effort to Satanise the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was literally translated, you could see what was said in the previous paragraph. I'm saying what people were talking about. That's what I'm saying. Talk. This, that the Croat side saw -- demonstrated its genocidal face, well, before the International Court of Justice, we had a case where we tried to prove that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender 6684 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 6684 will be Exhibit P3318.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your evidence, you've mentioned -- and in your statement various Croat actions that we've discussed, and you've argued that these jeopardized the Vance Plan. It was also the Serb side's actions that jeopardized the success of the Vance Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. It came from both sides. Who was the first and who was not, we could discuss that for days. It is a fact that after the Vance Plan, Croatia was always the first one to carry out these aggressions, Maslenica, the Miljevac Plateau, the Medak pocket, and then after that, Flash and Storm. Those are facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get P2870. This is tab 21, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a cable from Satish Nambiar to Marrack Goulding - these are UN representatives - dated 8 November 1992 regarding implementation of the Vance Plan. And at page 1.1, he says: "It is amply clear that notwithstanding all their assurances of co-operation and support for the Vance Plan and other associated Security Council resolutions, the Serb authorities in the UNPAs have implemented only those aspects of the plan that suited them and have blocked progress of further implementation to gain time for furtherance of other political and military objectives." That's correct, isn't it? That's correct, that that was actually happening in fact. I'm not asking you if it's correct that that's stated there. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written there. You are showing me things that are written and then you're asking me whether that is written there and then we see that that is written there. Now, if you're asking me for my own comment in this regard, then that that is completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: It is correct, in fact, that the Serb actions were pre -- they only implemented the aspects of the Vance Plan that suited them and they were doing so to gain time for the furtherance of political and military objectives; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, one could put it that way, but I explained to you yesterday. For example, after the Maslenica operation, Croatia did not carry out the Security Council resolution to go back. And Serbs also reacted in the following way: They did not want to return weapons to arms depots, that is to say, those that were under double lock where the Serb side and UNPROFOR had keys respectively. And then it could not be defended. That is one aspect. There are hundreds of others. We could go on and on enumerating all of that. It cannot be a mere yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: During the conflict in Croatia, you stated that the RSK Serbs refused to live together with Croats in any form whatsoever; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. Not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Can I --
