utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My statement is different. My statement is -- well, we should take a look at it and I know what the essence is, and I have been saying that all the time. It was a question of living together. Remember we talked about "suzivot" yesterday and the willingness of both sides is needed. We could not force the Croats to love us and live together with us. They were trying to expel us in every conceivable way. And we said many times that we could not live in the same state with Croats because they did not want to live with us. And that is the essence of my entire political work, if I can put it that way --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croats and Serbs can live together in the Republic of Serbian Krajina but we cannot live together in the same state.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak at a normal pace, slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If I could ask you to speak at a slower pace. Thank you. So do you confirm that you did state - and we'll get to the reasons behind this - but do you state -- you confirm that you did state that the Serbs refused to live together with the Croats in any form. You publicly stated this; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's asked an answered, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say "refused." I never said "refused." I never said that we refused that and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, if and when a counsel rises to put an objection on the record, please wait with your answer until the objection is resolved in one way or the other. That will be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, really. I was facing the Prosecutor and I didn't see the other side. I'm sorry. I am aware of that rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It's page 46, lines 18 to 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps if we go to the article now to speed things up and to go to his quote that I want to put onto the record. If we could get 6705. This is tab 57, page -- if we could turn to page 2. Now, this is an article in the "New York Times" dated 13 January 1995. And if we go to page 2, first line. And in B/C/S this is page 1, fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The first line we see: "'We don't want to be in Croatia in any form,' Savo Strbac, a minister in the self-styled government of the Krajina region, said recently. 'Our wish is to live with the other Serbs of the former Yugoslavia as we did for the past 70 years.'" You made that statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And, sir --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed that they conveyed it -- well, yes, the essence is what I talked about a moment ago. There is no reference to any kind of refusal whatsoever. We did not refuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could now go to 65 ter 6711.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. I haven't interrupted until now because there were a series of questions, but there are two transcript issues. At page 45, line 13, there was a fourth or at least there was a place mentioned that wasn't recorded on the transcript. And then at page 47 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let's do it case by case, Mr. Gosnell. 45:9?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I believe that there was one more aggression that was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Shall I attempt to clarify with the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, in answer to a previous question, you referred to Croatia carrying out aggressions to, and you mentioned, Maslenica, Miljevac Plateau, the Medak pocket, and then after that Flash and Storm. Was there any additional aggression that you wanted to mention?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, I mentioned Nos Kalik 2nd March 1992. Smaller than all the rest but it was the first one. Nos Kalik, it's a place against which an aggression has been committed after Krajina was placed under military protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The second one, Mr. President, is 47, line 2 -- 47, line 1. There is a place name mentioned there that was not mentioned by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Again, shall I attempt to clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in answer to another question, you said, "We could not force the Croats to" and it's written "Lovas" "and live together with us." Was there a place name that you mentioned when you said that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never mentioned "Lovas." No, I didn't mention a name at all. What does it have to do with anything? There's no logic to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I remember the -- the interpreter, the interpretation, where it is written "Lovas," it sounds a little bit similar in English but, of course, in B/C/S, the witness will not have a clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could it mean to leave us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, love us, to love us. That's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I believe this will be cleared up when the transcript is cleared up, and if not we could always review the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, if we could go now to another statement that you made publicly, and if we could get 6711. This is tab 63 on the monitor. And page 2, third paragraph. Now, this is from Agence Presse France, and I apologise we only have the English, but I'll read to you what it says: "'We have no choice,' insisted Savo Strbac, government secretary in the Serb Republic of Krajina proclaimed unilaterally in 1991 following an eight-month armed conflict with Croatia. 'It is out of the question for us to return to Croatia. Our final goal is union with other Serbs' (in Bosnia and the Republic of Serbia)." Do you remember making that statement?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's probably my statement. I keep repeating all the time. It says here for us to return to the state of Croatia. If you ask me why, I'll answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We will get to the reasons that you're giving for why.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We would tender these two articles, 6705 and 6711, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 6705 will be Exhibit P3319 and 6711 will be Exhibit P3320.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your statement on this topic, you acknowledge stating that the Serbs and Croats could not live together, and you claim that this meant they could not live in a single state. You said that you advocated from the statement "a predominantly Serb entity" but that this did not imply ethnic cleansing. Now, the predominantly Serb entity you were talking was the RSK either on its own or joined with other Serbian territories; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I meant primarily the RSK at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: To maintain a predominantly Serb entity, you would have to have a Serb majority ethnically in that territory, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, the pre-war population in SBWS - Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem - was majority Croat ethnicity, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I don't remember all the data because that was not my area. But in the district where I lived, Krajina, Banja, Lika Kordun and Dalmatia, Serbs were dominant before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Would you accept that in SBWS the Croats had a relative majority, not an absolute majority but a relative majority population-wise, and that Serbs were a considerable lesser per cent of the population. Would you accept that in the pre-war -- according to the pre-war 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's asked and answered, Mr. President. We got the same answer again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So you dispute that. Okay. Well, I'm going to put it to you that was the case and --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not disputing anything. Please do not put words in my mouth, words that I didn't say. I said I didn't live there and I cannot, off the cuff, remember the numbers. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get P2016. This is tab 35, page 9, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, I'll translate for you here. We have a table. It is on the B/C/S as well. And we can see that in Eastern Slavonia, this is the table at the top, Croats - and this is according to the pre-war composition - were 91.756, whereas Serbs were 67.742, and that equates to the Croats having approximately 46 per cent of the population. So do you accept that they did have a relative majority of the population, according to that census?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. I don't know what the question is. It's vague. Is the question that the witness is expected to say his comment on what's on this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm testing whether the witness, having been shown the statistics, is willing to accept this or whether he still disputes this. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do you still dispute --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not dispute anything. I haven't disputed anything so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I should have put that in the reverse, whether he would accept that those are the correct figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's a question you may put to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now you would have to explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Would you accept, seeing this table of the statistics, that the pre-war population of Eastern Slavonia had a relative majority of ethnic Croats?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept only what I see here with my own eyes. Whether it's true or not true, I'm not a demographer, an expert, to tell you whether it was accurate or not. There were many manipulation with the censuses and there were problems about defining Eastern Slavonia. Was it just the area held by the Serbs or was it something broader? In some places, UNPA areas were broader than what the Serbs held. It's difficult to say I accept or not. I can only accept that there were so many Serbs and so many Croats as is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If these figures are correct, then, in order to maintain your Serb-dominated entity in so far as SBWS is concerned, you would have to remove members of the ethnic Croat community; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are such logical answers. How shall I put it? I'm not an idiot. If you have one majority that you want to turn into a minority in order to create a different majority, then what you say is the only way. Unless you suddenly get the birth-rate of the Serbs to spike very fast, all of a sudden, to make them the majority and you have the Croats disappear, if this data is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to ask you some questions about your NGO, Veritas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, the last sentence of the witness was not transcribed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness has, so far, not been responsive to any of our pleas to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Did you hear that remark from the interpreters, Mr. Strbac?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, I was going to ask a question about your -- a series of questions about your NGO, which is Veritas. You're the head of that NGO; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, if the witness could repeat his last sentence on the previous answer, if he can recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And if he could answer my question, that would be helpful as well. Did you hear my question, Mr. Strbac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did. I don't hear what is said in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do I take it, then - and that's not a question for you, Mr. Strbac - that the interpreter's remark is not translated into B/C/S? Could I have an answer from the booth?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Well, the English interpreter said what she said, and we don't know if our colleagues interpreted it for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. What the interpreters said, Mr. Strbac - just one moment - is this: "The witness has, so far, not been responsive to any of our pleas to slow down." So they really have a problem. And I should think that, as a former professional judge, and even as a lawyer, you would -- you would be experienced in this kind of exercise, and you would be able to slow the pace of what you are saying, even if sometimes - and then I could understand - you're taken away by what you are trying to convey to us. But, in general, you should be able, as a professional, to slow the pace of what you are saying so that interpreters and court recorders can do their job efficiently. Now, Mr. Zivanovic, where is it that the witness -- that a sentence of the witness or a phrase of the witness has been lost in translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is in -- at page 54, line 6. The whole sentence was not transcribed, or -- or maybe not -- not translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I can clarify with the witness, if you'd like, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think you should re-read the entire answer he gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Anyway we'll ask the correction of official transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's perhaps even easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So now you may continue, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we get 65 ter 6710 - that's tab 62 - on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And, sir, this an is interview with Globus in March 2005. If we start by showing the front page, you recognise the person shown; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little, yes. That's a younger me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recall giving this interview to Globus in 2005?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There were hundreds of interviews. I probably gave one to them, too, at some point, but it's my photograph, so I suppose I did talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 of the English and B/C/S under the heading "Manipulation," you were asked whether you'd thought about registering crimes against Croats as well as crimes against Serbs, and your answer is: "Crimes against Croats were no secret in the first place. The cases of the suffering of Croats across the area of Knin were being followed by international teams, organisations ..." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated something like this many, many times, so I suppose I said it to them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Then if we turn to page 6 in the English, and this is B/C/S page 4, third column, on page 6 there's a heading "Croatian Policy 's Conscience" in the middle of the page. And at the end of your answer to that first question, it says: "Do not attack me - because I have never provided a single incorrect piece of data." Now, that's not correct, is it, that your claim that you never provided an incorrect piece of data is not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never intentionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: In fact, your organisation, Veritas, has and continues to convey incorrect information, including in terms of the list of Serb victims of Croatian crimes; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We provided information such as we have with the best intention of providing correct information. However, mistakes occur, and even today, we've made hundreds of mistakes. You cannot turn these mistakes into a rule. If a name is repeated, it could be a technical slip. You can't take it as intentional as was done in the International Court of Justice when two names were repeated out of 135, two names were duplicated, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: It was more than two names in that specific proceeding that were raised. There were at least five examples that were given of persons listed as Serbs killed by Croatian forces who were not, in fact, killed. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croats objected to two duplicated names in the trial in March before the International Court of Justice on a list of 7.135 names. In preparation for the trial, in these appeals and counter-appeals and responses and replies, a total of ten more objections were made on the Croatian side. The question was whether they were killed by Croats, by the enemy, or they got killed in the mutual settlement of scores or killing each other. Croats turned out to be right and we corrected that. At the same time, analysing their lists containing a thousand more names, there were 100 names actually less than -- 100 mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: In fact, you were correct that Croatia pointed out some errors, but some of these continue to feature on your list of Serb victims and I'll mention, for example, Mirko Rajsic. Now, he's still listed as there. He was killed in front of a tavern on 16 October 1993 in a traffic accident while driving his bicycle; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I knew that, that he was killed on a bicycle outside a cafe, I would have certainly placed him somewhere because our list is divided between direct and indirect victims. That's what we did in Veritas, and we were forced to do that by Croat objections in preparing for the International Court of Justice. Not all the victims are victims of genocide. There are victims of war, casualties of war, people who could have been killed while riding a bicycle, going to the front line or coming back from the front line, and such people are to be found in all lists - in Croatian lists, Serbian, Bosniak, and all sides. We have direct and indirect casualties. I can tell you what we presented to the ICJ; namely, that about 10 percent of indirect victims --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You've answered my question, that your list includes not just victims killed by the Serbs -- by the Croats, sorry, but you also include people who died, as you say, as a indirect cause of war. Now, you said before that you cannot turn --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. We are no different than other lists in the regions. We are even better, more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If you'd let me ask a question, you said before you cannot turn these mistakes into a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get 65 ter 6726. This is tab 78.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a chapter called "Storm JCE," and it's a chapter in a publication that you wrote, correct, "Storm JCE"? It's called -- in fact, the full title is "Storm Joint Criminal Enterprise," and this chapter is "Aggression, Scorched Earth Policy." You wrote this, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can go to page 5, heading 2.2.2, and this is page 6 in B/C/S. Now, if we look at heading 2.2.2, the last paragraph under that heading says: "Analysing Croatia commission's list, Veritas established that there were five living people among those identified as killed (meaning that other persons were buried under their names). Such a large incidence of mistaken identity throws doubt on the entire identification process by Croatian official organs of those who were killed in Operation Storm." Sir, in relation to your own list, you said that you could not turn these errors into a rule, but when it comes to the Croatian list, in fact, you said the opposite, that they undermine the credibility of their entire processes; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have to explain to you here that for the first time during Storm and Flash operations, protocols were submitted. Croatia did that under the pressure of the international community and submitted them to the Serbian side. The protocols contained a photograph of the person killed, a description, a description of clothing and footwear, and where the person died. In such precise protocols, we find five people who were still living. You have a photograph and then you mark it completely inaccurately. It's a very specific, very emphatic situation. We showed these photographs to the families, and the person is standing there alive. And he says, It's not me. And I answer, Well, if it's not you, it's somebody else. This is an idiosyncrasy of the protocols that the Croats gave us from that operation. That was not done previously in any other operation; that is to say, they did not earlier provide us with such protocols. And as for the JCE, I consulted the OTP, people from your own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They indicted Croatian generals for Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: -- you've gone beyond the question that I asked. The JCE issue goes beyond my question. Sir, the Office of the Prosecutor has never called you as a witness here at the Tribunal, has it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, that completes my questions. I would tender the Globus article, 65 ter 6710, for evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 6710 will be Exhibit P3321.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I do have some re-direct, Mr. President. Could I request the Court's indulgence to take the break now, in particular, so I can print out the transcript and have it to hand so I can make specific references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And how long would your re-direct take, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I certainly will not go beyond the end of the day as regularly scheduled, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The end of the day, minus 15 minutes for Judges' questions so that we can finish the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Strbac, we will take the break a little bit early. Still 30 minutes. So we will be back by 12.30. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [The witness stands down] 3100

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. May we have P998, please. Prosecution tab 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, Mr. Strbac, you were shown this document coming up on the screen of the minutes of the extraordinary session of the RSK Assembly in March 1993. If we could now turn to page 62 in the English and page 64 in the B/C/S, you were shown this ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You were shown this decision, and the Prosecutor asked you or put to you: "Hadzic's decision that we see of 17th March 1993 was a war-time decree; correct? It seems to be that way because a state of war was declared in January." Now, reading the first line of this excerpted decision in the minutes, it says: "Pursuant to Article 78, paragraph 1, item 1, of the constitution of the RSK, makes the following ..." Now, is Article 78(1)(i) of the RSK constitution the provision concerning war-time powers?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we look at the constitutional provision, we will see that that is not the case, that it speaks of peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At this point, then, could we have L3, page 22 of the English and page 6, going over to 7 of the B/C/S. "The president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, one, nominates candidates for the government members having heard the opinion of the majority in the Assembly ..." Now, having seen that, does that affect your opinion about the basis on which this particular decision was issued?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've already said that this has to do with peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And given that there's a specific reference to this provision, do you think that's relevant to understanding the basis on which it was issued?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that it was logical to refer to this article because - how do I put this? - it would too much if the head of state would appoint the prime minister-designate and the entire government even though there is a state of war on. I think that, in that way, all branches of government could not be functioning properly. Although it was war-time, after all, one should behave at least some moments as if were peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we return now to P998, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, again, Mr. Strbac, these are the minutes from March 1993 of the assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we now have page 66 in the B/C/S and page 66 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, this is in reference, Mr. Strbac, to a question that was put to you by the Prosecutor at page 10, and the question concerns Article 78(7) of the constitution. And then it says at line 4, this was the question to you, Mr. Strbac: "And the government acted pursuant to the authority that Hadzic delegated to it. For example, as you said in a decision in September 1993 concerning the appointment of judges in the RSK, that was based on his presidential decree from January; correct?" And your answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, first of all, looking at this section of the minutes from the assembly meeting, it says: "Moving on to the third item on the agenda, adoption of decree laws passed in time of war." And then at the bottom, in English anyway, it says: "Pursuant to Article 78, paragraph 7, of the constitution of the RSK, president of the republic shall pass the decree ..." And then if we could turn over the page in English and in B/C/S. And Article 1 concerns territorial jurisdiction of the courts and so forth. Now, is this decree relevant to the applicability of the president's decree that was made in January?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously not. I was explaining when I was responding to the Prosecutor's question that when somebody transfers his powers to someone else, he can at any point in time withdraw them. At least that's what I think. I'm not an expert. I mean, I'm not a theoretician as far as constitutional law is concerned. But by the very logic of things, that's the way it seems to be. It's like when you retain a lawyer to represent you. You can still give up on that and you can withdraw power of attorney, and so son.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you know whether this assembly meeting in March 1993 was the first assembly meeting after January 1993, when Operation Maslenica was launched?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know. I wouldn't want to speculate. But if you're asking me this, since it has to do with territorial jurisdiction of courts, that really does not involve war-time subject matter, the jurisdiction of courts in a state. Had it not been war-time, had there not been a state of war, somebody, I mean, would have to set the jurisdiction of courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's just turn over to the next page, and there it says: "Who votes for this decree passed by the president of the republic on the basis of a declaration of war? Does anyone mind? Does anyone offish acknowledging that the decree laws in a time of war are adopted by the assembly?" Now, does this procedure --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We need to turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes, can I just get a page reference in English? I'm trying to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In English, it's page 70 now. Page 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, you will remember, Mr. Strbac, and we discussed it, that Article 78(7) of the constitution says that: "Under his initiative," "his" being the president, "or under the government's proposal, during the state of war or immediate threat of war adopts acts about issues from the assembly's jurisdiction and is required to submit them before the assembly as soon as the assembly is able to meet."

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meet, yes. You asked me whether there were any assembly sessions from the decree in January until this, and then I told you that I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I hadn't actually come to my question yet, Mr. Strbac, and the question is simply this: Does this procedure that you see in the minutes accord with what appears to be prescribed and that you confirmed was prescribed by Article 78(7)?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to that be that way. If this is the first session - I assume it is, and I don't know whether there were any sessions in between - and precisely on the basis of what was done through this decree declaring a state of war, everything he did as far as courts were concerned, he gave to the assembly for their confirmation. That is shown by these minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with this particular document now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, at page 17 of today's transcript, you were asked some questions about allegations made by Mr. Martic against Mr. Hadzic in October 1993. Now, may I ask you: Was there any political background that you can recall that may have been relevant to those remarks? What was the political context, if any, of those remarks?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Martic from the very outset was within the structures of the Krajina government. In a way, I mean, he is a founder -- one of the founders of the Republic of the Serb Krajina, what was called the SAO Krajina at first. And it seems to me that he did not like it, the fact that Hadzic was appointed president of the state because now he became his superior, at least in terms of the office held; whereas Martic thought -- well, he'd succeed him later on because you could see that he had these aspirations to be the person in charge. I believe that there were some -- I mean, well, that it wasn't smooth sailing between the two of them, that Martic simply expressed that at this assembly and once or twice I think at government sessions when he said, Ah, they are not going to come to your sessions, to Knin, I mean from the eastern part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, in line 7, it is said I think -- "I think at government sessions when he said, Ah, he is not going to come to your sessions, to Knin ..." It seems that he said differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, I presume you had the intervention of my colleague translated. Was there something that you would wish to correct, having heard that intervention?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would not come. Martic was also a member of that government, I think. It was sort of like that, that's what he said, that he would not come to Knin. He would not come to Knin from the eastern part. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have 1D2523, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, you were asked questions about this document on page 26 and 25 of the transcript. Now, first of all, can you identify what this document is and who is its author?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The supreme military court. Its seat was in Belgrade and it was a court that dated back to the times of the SFRY. It was in Belgrade then and it was in Belgrade now. They were involved in proceedings against soldiers who had committed crimes in the area of the Republic of the Serb Krajina all the way up until 19th May 1992 when they officially left the area of the Republic of the Serb Krajina. Then the authorities -- I mean, well, then UNPROFOR came. That was part of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you said in response to the question by the Prosecutor at 26, line 16, "Do you stand by that it is permissible to kill civilians during a time of war?" And then your answer was: "This is just as the supreme military court took something out of context from my appeal, which was several hundred pages long." Now, can I first ask: Is it right that this, then, is a summary of --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not thousands, not thousands. Not even hundreds. No. Tens of pages. That's how appeals are written.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Okay. And is it right that this is a summary of the arguments that you made in those other documents?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of that. I've explained that in this appeal, I mean, that it was a passivist document. And I attacked the makers of war, the initiators of war, because in this case we can see who the victims are. Civilians are the victims. And these young people, soldiers, like this Gagic, he had just done his regular military service. And I said that if I could decide against wars and therefore against killings of soldiers and civilians and anyone else, after all, life is more valuable than anything else. But I acted as defence counsel there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, you said in your answer while being cross-examined by the Prosecutor that the court took something out of context. Now, as you sit here, can you think of any comment -- context that would be relevant to the issue of whether it is lawful to target civilians? What context or circumstances might be relevant to that, as you sit here?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember this case correctly, this young soldier was brought to the front line, and his superiors told him, Everything that is on the other side is your enemy. This soldier crossed the front line himself and whoever he found there, this elderly married couple, he killed them. And he returned, running, shouting, yoo hoo hoo, I've just killed two Ustashas. You see, I asked for a psychiatric evaluation to see whether he was competent at all when he committed that crime, and you see that that was also accepted by the court, and they ordered that this evidence be adduced at re-trial. Through my appeal, I defended all of these young people who were forced to shoot and kill somewhere. I wanted then, and that is my wish to this day, that those who forced them to wage war and kill be brought before courts of law. That was the essence of my appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At page 53 today, you were asked some questions about the pre-war ethnic composition of the territory that subsequently became the RSK. And I should correct myself. You were actually asked about the SBWS only. Now, first of all --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- can you say whether the pre-war population of the RSK, taken as a totality, had more Serbs or more Croats?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand. Do you mean the entire Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No. The question was just about the RSK. And whether or not taking --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, the RSK had more Serbs, which could be seen from that table that was produced here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you were asked a hypothetical about the majority in a particular region, if they are of a particular ethnicity, about the means of changing that composition. Does it also depend on how you define the geographic entity?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I tried to explain. I think that I succeeded in saying that there were different interpretations as to what a certain region represents in territorial terms, and then everyone paints their picture and then, of course, one has to take into account the population as well. I know Western Slavonia rather than Eastern Slavonia, and I know that according to the Vance Plan, twice as much territory was supposed to be there rather than was actually in the hands of the Serbs. My counting was that there were only 15.000 in the area that was held under Serb control rather than 30.000. I did not deal with Eastern Slavonia, and I cannot tell you about that right now because I didn't deal with it. But I'm giving you the figures at the time of Operation Flash.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That concludes my examination and re-direct, Mr. President. Thank you very much, Mr. Strbac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, I have one question; perhaps a few sub-questions. At the beginning of your testimony, you told us that the Croat authorities, and I quote, "... asked me to sign some kind of statement of loyalty to the new state and even worse things were asked," indicating that asking from a judge for a statement of loyalty to the new state is a bad thing. Could I ask you, who appointed you judge of the municipal court of Benkovac in 1977?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. And when you took that position in 1977, were you asked to make some sort of statement of loyalty to the state or to the entity within which you were to function as a judge?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that form. One only took the solemn oath, a solemn undertaking that I would enforce the law, the kind of oath that exists in every country before the president of the assembly. Let me just add that when I became a judge of the district court, then it was the National Assembly of Croatia that appointed me to that position. It all depended on the ranking of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. That would have been my next question about, indeed, the district court. So it's the National Assembly of Croatia. And then a similar kind of statement or oath?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an oath. The president of the assembly would call however many we were who were appointed, and after that appointment, we made in a chorus a solemn declaration that I will honourably comply with and enforce the laws, et cetera. But this was something quite different. The authorities changed. There were new elections. And they foisted it on us Serbs, only Serbs - at that time I had been a judge for two and a half years - at that time they foisted on us who were of Serb ethnicity a declaration that we would be loyal to the state of Croatia. So it was not asked of everybody. Just of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the same session and today as well, you told us about the fact that the RSK - and that is either the assembly or the government - also appointed judges. You remember that, do you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed the minutes of the sessions of the government and the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now, my question is: Did these new-appointed judges have to pledge their loyalty to the newly established RSK.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that way and not with that document. It was done in the way we worked. Whoever elected you or appointed you, you would take a solemn oath only in the sense that you would, in the best possible way, to the best of your ability and honourably, perform your judicial duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If there are no follow-up questions, Mr. Strbac, we thank you very much for coming to The Hague to assist us. This is the end of your testimony. You're now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back home. The court usher will escort you out of court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If there's nothing else, court is adjourned for the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
